tier_reason: The README Benchmarks table compares SNKV directly against SQLite (WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, 8 MB cache, 4 KB pages, WITHOUT ROWID), and every claimed number matches. The code is public (tests/test_benchmark.c and the separate hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv repo), but no CPU model, compiler version or build mode is stated, so these are first-party numbers with partial methodology: tier C. The Makefiles suggest both sides may be -O0 builds, which would also cap it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 1.64x-2x faster than SQLite (1M records): sequential writes 232K vs 142K ops/s (1.64x), random reads 160K vs 90K ops/s (1.77x), sequential scan 2.89M vs 1.56M ops/s (1.85x), random updates 31K vs 16K ops/s (1.9x), random deletes 31K vs 16K ops/s (~2x), mixed workload 62K vs 34K ops/s (1.79x).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated with the results. SNKV Makefile: gcc, default BUILD=debug (-g -O0 -DDEBUG), BUILD=release gives -O2 -DNDEBUG. The SQLite comparison repo (hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv) Makefile: gcc -g -Wall with no -O flag, i.e. GCC's default -O0.
corrections.caveats: The SNKV side comes from tests/test_benchmark.c. The SQLite side comes from a separate 0-star repo, hash-anu/sqllite-benchmark-kv, whose README only says 'run make test'. No CPU model, compiler version or build mode is stated. That repo compiles sqlite3.c with gcc -g -Wall and no optimization flag (-O0), and SNKV's Makefile defaults to a -O0 debug build, so both sides may have been unoptimized; the result may not hold at -O2/-O3. SNKV is SQLite's own B-tree/pager/WAL with the SQL parser, planner and VDBE removed, so the gain is from skipping the SQL layer, not from a faster storage engine. The linked LMDB and RocksDB comparison repos (hash-anu/lmdb-benchmark, hash-anu/rocksdb-benchmark) contain only source code and no published numbers; the README itself suggests RocksDB for maximum write throughput and LMDB for maximum read speed.

notes: Metadata checks out via gh: Apache-2.0, 78 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-26, so active. The main new finding is that both benchmark builds default to -O0; tier stays C.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed PVLDB 15(3) paper (arXiv extended version) that compares APEX directly against FAST+FAIR and five other PM indexes, and states GCC 10.2 and a Xeon Gold 6252; the repo's CMakeLists.txt gives the flags. It is not tier A because the public harness (src/benchmark/main.cpp) only builds APEX (index_type == "apex"). The competitor code, including the authors' own range-scan additions for FAST+FAIR, LB+-Tree and uTree and their LB+-Tree fix, is only linked to the upstream repos, so the comparison against the baseline cannot be rerun from public code.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-thread results (paper Fig. 4). Inserts: up to 15x/2.7x/3.8x/1.66x/6.8x/3.7x faster than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree across five datasets (up to 3.8x over FAST+FAIR). On the hardest-to-fit FB dataset, inserts are 1.18x/5.16x/2.3x/1.26x faster than FAST+FAIR/BzTree/uTree/FPTree but 5.77%/42% slower than LB+-Tree/DPTree. Search: up to 7.1x/3.9x/4.1x/3.2x/3.2x/5.8x higher than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree. Scans: up to 7.6x/1.45x/1.46x/1.83x/16.38x/3.1x faster than BzTree/LB+-Tree/FAST+FAIR/DPTree/uTree/FPTree on five datasets. The abstract says up to ~15x better than existing PM indexes; that figure is the BzTree insert case.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.2 'with all optimizations' (paper section 6.2). The repo's CMakeLists.txt GCC flags are -mrtm -msse4.1 -mavx2 -O3 -g -march=native.
corrections.hardware: 2.1GHz Intel Xeon Gold 6252 (24 cores / 48 hyperthreads, 35.75MB L3), 768GB Intel Optane DCPMM (6 x 128GB) plus 192GB DRAM, Arch Linux kernel 5.10.11
corrections.stars_or_usage: 49 stars. Built on Microsoft's ALEX learned index code (README). Published as PVLDB 15(3):597-610 (Nov 2021, DOI 10.14778/3494124.3494141).
corrections.caveats: All comparisons are against other PM-resident indexes on real Optane DCPMM, not against DRAM-resident RocksDB/LevelDB/LMDB or the RMI/PGM learned indexes. The public repo's benchmark only runs APEX; competitor implementations, including the authors' added range scans for FAST+FAIR, LB+-Tree and uTree and their LB+-Tree fix, are only linked to upstream repos. APEX is slower than LB+-Tree and DPTree on inserts for the FB dataset. Intel Optane DCPMM has been discontinued, so the target hardware is no longer sold.

notes: Numbers are accurate, but the record's '15x' was presented as a general insert result; it is the BzTree case, and the insert gain over FAST+FAIR is 3.8x. I added the FB insert regression. Downgraded A to B because baseline code is missing from the artifact. Metadata checks out via gh: MIT, not a fork, last commit 2023-04-19, so abandoned.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed PVLDB 13(4) paper comparing DPTree directly against FAST+FAIR, FPTree and WORT, and it states g++ 6.4 -O3 and 2x Xeon Platinum 8263C. It is not tier A because the public repo only has DPTree's own drivers (test/dptree_test.cxx, test/concur_dptree_test.cxx). The FAST+FAIR/WORT harness, the authors' FPTree reimplementation and their added FAST+FAIR concurrent-update code are not published, so the comparison cannot be reproduced.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-thread micro-benchmark (25M-100M random 64-bit keys). Point lookups: up to 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x faster than FAST+FAIR/FPTree/WORT. Inserts: 1.27-1.43x lower latency than FAST+FAIR and 1.76-1.78x lower than FPTree. Range scans: up to 3.0x/10.98x faster than FPTree/WORT but up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR. Concurrent YCSB (50M keys, up to 32 threads). InsertOnly: up to 1.36x higher throughput than FAST+FAIR at 32 threads. ReadOnly: 1.32-1.58x (vs FAST+FAIR) and 1.37-1.7x (vs FPTree) higher throughput. ReadUpdate: highest throughput at all thread counts, up to 1.7-5.07x over the other indexes. ScanInsert: FAST+FAIR keeps the highest scan throughput.
corrections.hardware: Two Intel Xeon Platinum 8263C @ 2.50GHz (26 physical cores), 35MB LLC, 376GB DRAM, 512GB Intel Optane DC PMM in App Direct mode via ext4-DAX, Linux kernel 4.9. All threads bound to one socket.
corrections.workload: Single-thread micro-benchmark: 64-bit random integer keys, 16-byte key-value pairs, 25M-100M keys; insert latency, point lookup, and range scan at 0.001%-0.1% selectivity. Concurrent YCSB-style workloads on 50M keys: InsertOnly, ReadOnly, ReadUpdate (50/50), ScanInsert (95% scans/5% inserts) and Mixed, up to 32 threads on one socket, on real Intel Optane DC PMM.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 61 stars; published as PVLDB 13(4):421-434 (Dec 2019, DOI 10.14778/3372716.3372717; presented at VLDB 2020)
corrections.caveats: The 1.82x/1.85x/2.19x figures are single-thread point-lookup gains over FAST+FAIR/FPTree/WORT respectively, not gains over FAST+FAIR across workloads. The 3.0x/10.98x figures are range-scan gains over FPTree/WORT; on scans DPTree is up to 1.1x slower than FAST+FAIR, which also keeps the highest scan throughput in ScanInsert. Experiments ran on real Optane DC PMM (App Direct, ext4-DAX), not emulated PM. FPTree is the authors' own reimplementation because the original is closed-source. The public repo contains only DPTree's own benchmark drivers, not the baseline harness. Intel Optane is discontinued.

notes: The record misattributed the speedup triple (the 1.82/1.85/2.19 figures are point lookups against three different indexes). It wrongly called the compiler string garbled (it is g++ 6.4 -O3) and guessed emulated PM (the paper used real Optane). The page range is 421-434, not 421-433. Downgraded A to B because baseline code is not public. Metadata checks out via gh: MIT, 61 stars, not a fork, last commit 2021-07-28, so abandoned.
